title: 10 - Western Political Thought

content.text: Syllabus — Western Political Thought: Plato, Aristotle, Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke, John S. Mill, Marx, Gramsci, Hannah Arendt. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 10)

the canon of Western political thinkers — Plato, Aristotle, Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke, J.S. Mill, Marx, Gramsci and Hannah Arendt — their central ideas, the comparisons the syllabus draws (Plato vs Aristotle, Hobbes vs Locke, Marx vs Gramsci) and their critiques.

Plato (justice, philosopher-king, Popper critique), Aristotle (constitutions, revolution), Machiavelli (realism, virtu-fortuna), Hobbes (Leviathan, sovereignty), Locke (natural rights, limited state), Mill (liberty, harm principle), Marx (materialism, alienation, surplus value), Gramsci (hegemony), Arendt (vita activa, banality of evil).
Q — Examine Plato’s conception of justice, education, communism and the philosopher-king, and evaluate Popper’s charge that ‘Plato was an enemy of the open society’. (UPSC 2015)
Build Plato’s ideal state — justice, education, philosopher-king, communism — and then judge whether it really amounts to totalitarianism.
— functional harmony, ‘one man, one job’: each class does its own task and no other.
(The doctor heals, the soldier guards, the farmer farms; injustice is the farmer trying to command the army.)
2. Soul and the myth of metals
(Gold, silver and bronze souls — yet a bronze father may have a gold son, so birth is not destiny.)
‘The state is the individual writ large’.
— a lifelong sieve ending at 50 in rule by the wise.

(Allegory of the cave: prisoners mistake shadows on the wall for reality; only he who has left the cave and seen the sun may rule — as one wants the trained navigator at the helm, not the loudest sailor.)
— no private property or family for the two ruling classes only.
(A judge who owns no shares in the company before him, and no son to favour, cannot be bought.)
(Censorship of poets and state-arranged breeding — the closed society in miniature.)
: all Western philosophy is ‘footnotes to Plato’.
defines justice as ‘each element in society doing its appropriate task, doing it well and doing it only’ — a

rather than a legal rule. On this ‘one man, one job’ principle the doctor heals, the soldier guards and the farmer produces; injustice is meddling, the farmer presuming to command the army. Justice is thus ‘the architectonic principle’ that holds the whole polis together.
2. Soul and the myth of metals.
The state mirrors the soul: its three parts —
— correspond to rulers, guardians and producers, since ‘the state is the individual writ large’. The

legitimises this order as a ‘noble lie’: men are born with gold, silver or bronze in their souls. Crucially the scheme is not hereditary caste — a bronze artisan’s gifted son may be promoted to gold, so function, not birth, fixes rank.
, a lifelong sieve culminating at fifty in the rule of the
— ‘until philosophers are rulers or rulers learn philosophy, there is no end to the ills of states’. The

supplies the justification: chained prisoners take flickering shadows for reality, and only the philosopher who has climbed out and seen the sun knows the Form of the Good. Hence ‘it is foolish to limit an expert physician with the book of medicine’ — the philosopher-king rules by wisdom, not by law.
To free the rulers from private temptation, Plato prescribes
communism of property and of wives

— but only for the two upper classes, the producers keeping both. The logic is the modern conflict-of-interest rule: a judge who owns no shares in the company before him, and has no son to promote, cannot be bought. It is therefore an ‘economic solution to a political ailment’, unlike
The Open Society and Its Enemies
, holds that ‘Plato was an enemy of the open society’: a rigid class order, censorship of poets and music, state-arranged breeding, and rule by an unaccountable elite add up to
. Above all Plato sought to ‘arrest all political change’ — ‘change is evil, rest divine’ — which is the mark of the closed society.
The charge is powerful but arguably anachronistic, reading twentieth-century fascism back into a fourth-century BC moral treatise;

replies that ‘fascism and Platonism are incomparable’, for Plato’s rulers hold no property and seek no glory. Whatever the verdict, his linkage of knowledge, virtue and rule remains the founding statement of political philosophy — all Western philosophy, said
Q — Analyse Aristotle’s critique of Plato’s idealism, and contrast their theories of justice and the state. (UPSC 2019)
Show how the pupil demolished the teacher — on Forms, on ‘one man, one job’ and communism — and then set their justice and state side by side.
— idealism gives way to empirical realism.
(Plato designs the state he wishes existed; Aristotle collects 158 constitutions that actually exist.)
‘Plato is my friend, but truth is a greater friend’.
— a separate ‘world of ideas’ is unreal; the essence lies inside the thing.
(There is no perfect Chair in heaven — only chairs, studied and classified.)
3. Against ‘one man, one job’ and communism
(‘What is common to the greatest number gets the least care’ — like a shared hostel kitchen nobody cleans.)
— Plato: inner, moral, duty-based; Aristotle: external, legal,
(Equal pay for equal work, but higher office for higher merit — the seed of reservation debates.)
— both make it the school of the good life, but Plato perfects an ideal, Aristotle improves the actual.
(Philosopher-king vs rule of law and a middle-class polity.)
— realism corrects idealism; hence Aristotle, not Plato, is the ‘father of political science’.
was Plato’s pupil for twenty years and ‘rectified the limitations of Plato’s ideas’ by replacing idealism with

. Where Plato deduces the state he wishes existed from the Form of the Good, Aristotle collects and dissects 158 actual constitutions. The method is captured in ‘Plato is my friend, but truth is a greater friend’ — or, as
puts it, ‘as Brutus loved Rome more, so for Aristotle dear is Plato, but dearer is truth’.

— the claim that a separate, changeless ‘world of ideas’ is more real than the world we inhabit. For him the essence of a thing lies within the thing itself: there is no perfect Chair in heaven, only chairs to be observed, compared and classified. Politics accordingly becomes a practical science of what is attainable for men as they are, not a contemplation of an unrealisable ideal.
3. Against ‘one man, one job’ and communism.
Plato’s functional justice is faulted as
, too subjective and moral rather than legal, and as stressing duties while ignoring rights. His

fares worse: ‘what is common to the greatest number gets the least care’ — everyone’s property is no one’s responsibility, as in a shared hostel kitchen nobody cleans. Aristotle defends private property as the spur to effort and the family as a ‘time-tested institution’ of emotional stability.
— the harmony of the soul, a matter of performing duties. For Aristotle it is

: ‘it is unjust to treat equals unequally and unequals equally’. Equal work earns equal pay, but greater merit earns greater office — the ancestor of every modern argument over merit and compensatory discrimination. He splits it into

Both hold the state essential to the good life — Plato aims at ‘the greatest happiness of the whole’, Aristotle declares ‘man is by nature a political animal’ and the state exists ‘for the sake of the good life’. But Plato is the
who designs an ideal polis ruled by philosopher-kings above the law, while Aristotle is the
who prefers the rule of law and a middle-class ‘polity’ as the most stable attainable form.

Aristotle’s realism corrects Plato’s idealism — the shift is from an ideal to be constructed to institutions to be observed, compared and improved — which is why he, and not Plato, is called the ‘father of political science’. Yet the correction is internal to a shared Socratic conviction: the state exists not for mere life but for human excellence.
Q — Explain Aristotle’s classification of constitutions, his theory of proportionate equality and revolution, and assess his contribution to modern constitutional democracy. (UPSC 2021/2017)
Give the two criteria and the six forms, defend polity, then link proportionate equality and the causes of revolution to modern constitutionalism.
— how many rule, and for whose benefit.
(A single ruler serving the people is a king; the same man serving himself is a tyrant.)
(For Aristotle ‘democracy’ is the perverted form — rule by the poor in their own interest.)
— the middle class buffers rich and poor.
(A society of billionaires and beggars flips between oligarchy and mob rule; a large middle class steadies it.)
— equals equally, unequals unequally in proportion.
(Distributive: offices by merit; corrective: the court restores what was taken, whoever the parties are.)
— ‘the feeling of inequality, real or imagined, is the cause of revolution’.
(Perception is enough: a group that merely believes it is being denied its due will rebel.)
— rule of law, mixed government and stability seed modern constitutionalism, though his exclusions must go.
, the ‘father of comparative politics’, who with his students examined 158 constitutions, classifies governments on two axes: the
— one, few or many — and the

, whether the common good or the rulers’ own interest. The second is decisive: one man ruling for his people is a king, the same man ruling for himself is a tyrant. Form alone never settles legitimacy.
The cross-classification yields three correct forms and their perversions: rule by one —
. The last pair surprises modern readers: for Aristotle ‘democracy’ is the debased form, rule by the poor majority in their own class interest, whereas polity is the many ruling for the common good.
Polity is the ‘golden mean’ between oligarchy and democracy, and Aristotle identifies it with the

. Neither so rich as to be arrogant nor so poor as to be servile, it is the class most amenable to reason and to law. A society polarised between billionaires and beggars oscillates between oligarchy and mob rule; a broad middle stratum moderates the conflict and makes the constitution both stable and practicable — the best form for most states most of the time.
Justice requires ‘treating equals equally and unequals unequally in proportion to their inequalities’ —
, which allots honours and offices according to merit and contribution to the polis, and
, which simply restores what has been wrongly taken, treating the parties as arithmetically equal. The distinction remains the backbone of every argument about equity versus formal equality.

‘The feeling of inequality, real or imagined, is the cause of revolution’, and ‘poverty is the parent of revolution and crime’. The insight is psychological rather than economic: perception suffices, so a group that merely believes it is denied its due will revolt. Aristotle catalogues general and regime-specific causes and cures, counselling moderation, obedience to law, and enlargement of the middle class — a conservative concern for

over the rule of persons — ‘law is reason without passion’ — his mixed, middle-class polity and his focus on constitutional stability directly anticipate modern constitutional democracy, and reach India through the basic-structure idea of a government limited by law. His exclusion of women, workers and slaves from citizenship is ‘unacceptable in modern times’; democratise the citizen body and the framework survives intact.
Q — Critically examine Machiavelli’s separation of politics from ethics and religion, and his place in the evolution of political science. (UPSC 2018/2014)
Explain why he cuts politics loose from morality and the Church, then judge what that did for the discipline.
— men are selfish and fickle, so theorise them as they are.
(‘Men sooner forget the death of their father than the loss of their patrimony’.)
2. Politics vs ethics — the lion and the fox
— the prince ‘needs to know how to be bad’.
(The lion frightens off wolves but walks into traps; the fox sees the trap but cannot fight wolves — a ruler needs force and cunning together.)
(Fortuna is a river in flood: dykes built in calm weather — virtu — decide whether it drowns you.)
— religion is a tool of civic discipline: ‘use religion, don’t get used by it’.
(An oath binds a soldier where a wage will not.)
— the empirical method applied to states ‘as they are, not as they ought to be’;
amid the chaos of Renaissance Italy,

on a bleak reading of human nature: men are ungrateful, fickle and acquisitive, and ‘sooner forget the death of their father than the loss of their patrimony’. Political theory must therefore be built on men as they are, not as scripture wishes them to be — the first premise of every subsequent realist, from Hobbes to Morgenthau.
2. Politics vs ethics — the lion and the fox.
rather than morality, he holds that the prince ‘needs to know how to be bad rather than good’ and must combine ‘the courage of the

’, changing colours ‘like a chameleon’. The image is exact: the lion frightens off wolves but blunders into traps, the fox spots the trap but cannot fight wolves — force without guile, or guile without force, both fail. Hence, on the safer bet, ‘it is better for a prince to be
— not Christian virtue but energy, foresight and manly skill — contending with

, the element of chance in politics. Machiavelli likens fortuna to a river in flood: it cannot be abolished, but embankments raised in calm weather decide whether it drowns you. Roughly half of human affairs is thus governed by fortune and half left to our own control — a rejection of both divine providence and fatalism.

: not as truth to be obeyed but as a unifying, disciplining force to be managed, so that the ruler should ‘use religion rather than get used by it’. An oath binds a soldier where a wage will not, and Roman civic religion made citizens brave, whereas Christian otherworldliness had, he thought, made Italians weak. This subordination of Church to state makes him the ‘father of European secularism’.

to human affairs — studying states ‘as they are, not as they ought to be’ and reasoning from Roman and Italian example — Machiavelli breaks decisively with medieval theology and makes politics an autonomous, observable domain.
therefore called him ‘the Galileo of politics’; if Machiavelli was Copernicus,
was the Galileo of political theory.
He is condemned as ‘the most universally reprobated figure’ (
), an amoral cynic who licenses cruelty;
finds him ‘narrowly dated and narrowly located’ in the Italy of city-state warfare; and
saw the divorce of ethics from politics as a ‘death trap’. Yet the realism endures because it describes practice: as
observed, ‘everyone practises Machiavellism without confessing it’.
Q — Discuss Hobbes’ derivation of the state from human nature and the state of nature, his theory of absolute sovereignty and political obligation, and compare him with Machiavelli. (UPSC 2017)
Trace the chain — human nature to state of nature to contract to absolute sovereign — then say how this differs from Machiavelli’s realism.
— ‘an endless desire for power after power that ceases only in death’, driven by fear.
(‘Fear and I were born twins’ — Hobbes was born as the Armada approached.)
— a ‘war of every man against every man’; life ‘solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short’.
(Not a jungle but a blackout riot: no police, so even the peaceable arm themselves first.)
— all with all, surrendering every right at once; society and state are born together.
(The sovereign is not a party, so he can breach nothing.)
— ‘absolute, indivisible, inalienable, perpetual’; ‘covenants without the sword are but words’.
(No division of powers: a Leviathan cut in two is two civil wars.)
— total and irrevocable, yet resting on
(A conscript may flee the battlefield; if the state cannot protect you, it cannot command you.)
— advice to a prince versus a deductive science of the state;
Using the ‘resolutive-compositive’ method borrowed from Galileo — break society into its parts, then rebuild it —
. Man is matter in motion, selfish and materialistic, marked by ‘an endless desire for power after power that ceases only in death’, and above all governed by
. Born as the Spanish Armada approached, he wrote that ‘fear and I were born twins’ — fear is the engine of the whole system.
Absent a common power to keep men in awe, natural equality of ability breeds equality of hope, and hope breeds conflict: the result is a
‘war of every man against every man’

fuelled by competition, diffidence and glory, in which life is ‘solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short’. It is less a jungle than a city blackout: with no police, even the peaceable must strike first to be safe. Right and wrong have no place; there is only right of nature to everything.
Escape comes through reason — the laws of nature counselling peace — executed by a
in which each man covenants with every other, not with the ruler, to surrender

his natural rights to a common power. Society and state are thus created in one stroke, with no pre-political community as in Locke. Because the sovereign is not a party to the covenant, he can never be accused of breaching it — the device that makes his power unchallengeable.
— ‘that mortal god’ — is ‘absolute, indivisible, inalienable and perpetual’, at once legislator, judge and head of the church. ‘Law is the command of the sovereign’, anticipating
’s legal positivism, and ‘covenants without the sword are but words and of no strength to secure a man at all’. Division of powers is fatal: a Leviathan cut in two is simply two civil wars.
Since the covenant binds subjects to one another, obligation to obey is
; there is no right of revolt and ‘liberty exists where the law is silent’. Yet the whole edifice rests on consent given for

, so the one right that cannot be alienated is the right to life: a condemned man may resist and a conscript may flee the battlefield. If the sovereign cannot protect, he cannot command — protection and obedience are reciprocal.
who reject natural sociability and moralised politics, but
whose end is glory and survival, while
of the state whose end is escape from the state of nature.
reads him as the theorist of ‘possessive individualism’ fitting a market society — yet by grounding authority in consent, Hobbes is paradoxically a father of modern individualism.
Q — Evaluate Locke as the father of liberalism through his two contracts, natural rights, labour theory of property and toleration; and contrast with Hobbes on how each legitimizes state authority.
Show how Locke’s milder premises produce a limited state, then set his justification of authority against Hobbes’s point by point.
— peaceful and social, spoilt only by two ‘inconveniences’.
(No impartial judge: even an honest man judging his own boundary dispute will overvalue his claim.)
— one creates society, a second creates government by consent.
(Society survives the fall of a government, as a nation outlives a dissolved Parliament.)
3. Natural rights and the trust state
— life, liberty and property are retained, not surrendered; power is a
(A trustee who loots the estate is dismissed — hence the right of revolution.)
— ‘property is the product of one’s labour’, limited by spoilage and ‘enough and as good’ left for others.
(The apple is mine because I picked it, not because the king granted it.)
— the magistrate has no jurisdiction over the soul.
(But not for atheists, whose oaths he thought worthless.)
— absolute versus limited: ‘liberty where the law is silent’ against ‘no law, no liberty’.
, the ‘father of liberalism’, begins from a
in which reason — the law of nature — teaches men ‘not to harm others in their life, liberty and property’. His
is therefore ‘a state of peace and mutual assistance’, pre-political but not pre-social, flawed only by two
: each man judges his own cause, and passion distorts punishment. Even an honest man judging his own boundary dispute overvalues his claim — so an impartial judge, not a Leviathan, is what is wanted.
: the first constitutes civil society, the second institutes a government by

, to which they transfer only the powers to make, execute and adjudicate law. The separation matters constitutionally: because society precedes government, the fall of a government does not dissolve the community — a nation outlives a dissolved Parliament — and a people may replace its rulers without returning to anarchy.
3. Natural rights and the trust state.
are inalienable and are carried into civil society, not surrendered to it. The state therefore holds

, never original power: a ‘night-watchman’ state whose ‘sole purpose is the protection of property’, organised through separated legislative, executive and federative powers with the legislature supreme. A trustee who loots the estate is dismissed — which is precisely Locke’s

Property is pre-political and moral: ‘every man has a property in his own person’, so by mixing his labour with nature he makes a thing his own. The apple is mine because I picked it, not because the sovereign granted it. Two limits apply — no accumulation beyond what one can use without
, and ‘enough and as good’ must be left for others — though the invention of money quietly relaxes both, which is why
reads him as legitimising unlimited accumulation.

, Locke separates the ends of the state from those of the church: the magistrate governs ‘civil interests’ alone and has no jurisdiction over the soul, since belief cannot be coerced into existence by force. The principle is the seed of the modern secular state and of freedom of conscience — though he notoriously excludes atheists, whose oaths he thought worthless, and Catholics, as owing allegiance abroad.
Both argue from contract, but from opposite premises:
— a war-like state of nature, a
sovereign, ‘liberty where the law is silent’;

state, ‘where there is no law there is no liberty’. Hobbes legitimises authority as absolute to escape chaos; Locke legitimises it as limited and accountable to secure pre-existing rights — founding the liberal-constitutional tradition that runs to Rawls.

Q — Assess Mill’s harm principle and defence of free expression, his status as a ‘reluctant democrat’, and his case for the equality of women, within his revision of utilitarianism. (UPSC 2014/2018/2021)
Four demands in one: how he rewrote utilitarianism, and how liberty, democracy and women’s equality follow from it.
— pleasures differ in kind, not only in quantity.
(‘Better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied’ — poetry outranks pushpin, rescuing Bentham from the ‘pig’s philosophy’.)
— your liberty ends only where it harms another.
(Drinking alone is self-regarding and free; drunk driving harms others and may be punished.)
— ‘all silencing of discussion is an assumption of infallibility’.
(Even one dissenter must be heard: the silenced opinion may be true, or hold part of the truth.)
and prescribes plural voting and PR.
(A graduate’s extra vote — quality checking mere numbers.)
— legal subordination is ‘one of the chief hindrances to human improvement’.
(‘There remains no legal slave save the mistress of every house’.)

dimension: pleasures differ in kind, and those who have known both prefer the higher — ‘it is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied’. Against
claim that pushpin equals poetry if the quantity of pleasure is equal, this restores a standard of human excellence and disarms the charge of a ‘pig’s philosophy’.
Mill gives liberty priority: ‘over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign’. The

holds that ‘the sole end for which mankind is warranted in interfering with the liberty of a person is to prevent harm to others’ — a man’s own good is never sufficient warrant. Drinking alone is self-regarding and free; drunk driving is other-regarding and punishable. Liberty ends exactly where it harms another.

Mill’s defence of discussion is absolute: ‘all silencing of discussion is an assumption of infallibility’, and if all mankind minus one held an opinion, mankind would be no more justified in silencing that one than he in silencing mankind. The silenced view may be true; if false, truth held unchallenged decays into ‘dead dogma’; usually each side holds part of the truth. Hence his defence of the eccentric ‘crank’, whose rare genius benefits mankind.
: he accepts representative government as the ideal form yet fears the
— the social coercion of opinion that
. His safeguards favour quality over mere numbers: plural or weighted voting for the educated, proportional representation to protect minorities, open ballot, and a strong second chamber.

influence, Mill attacks the legal subordination of women as ‘one of the chief hindrances to human improvement’ and observes that ‘there remains no legal slave save the mistress of every house’. Equality would end the family as ‘a school of despotism’, make it instead a school of sympathy, and ‘double the mass of mental faculties available for the higher service of humanity’. He moved the first parliamentary amendment for women’s suffrage.
Mill is the ‘first serious liberal democrat’ (
), balancing utility with liberty, majority rule with minority rights, and individuality with social progress.

faults the self- and other-regarding distinction as untenable — no act is purely private — making him a ‘prophet of an empty liberty’; yet the harm principle remains the working test of state interference in every modern debate on censorship, privacy and personal choice.

Q — Discuss Marx’s base-superstructure model, class and class struggle, and alienation; and how Gramsci’s concepts of hegemony, the integral state and organic intellectuals rescued Marxism from economic determinism. (UPSC 2015/2016/2020 + Gramsci 2013/2016/2019)
First lay out classical Marxism, then show precisely which of its defects Gramsci repairs and how.
— who owns production shapes law, politics and ideas.
(‘To think we must live, to live we must eat, and to eat we must produce’ — the factory explains the courtroom.)
— labour alone creates value; the capitalist pockets the unpaid remainder.
(Paid for four hours, worked for eight — the other four are profit.)
— estrangement from the product, the process, others and oneself.
(The assembly-line worker who fits one bolt all day owns nothing he makes and recognises nothing of himself in it.)
4. Class in itself to class for itself
— revolution needs consciousness, not just misery.
(Millions of workers are a statistic; an organised, self-aware proletariat is a force.)
But the predicted revolution never came.
— rule by consent through civil society, the ‘integral state’.
(School, press and church make inequality look like common sense — so fight a
led by organic intellectuals before the war of manoeuvre.)
— the decisive battlefield shifts from economics to culture; determinism is repaired, not abandoned.
— the forces and relations of production — conditions the

of law, state, religion and ideas: ‘in order to think we must live, to live we must eat, and to eat we must produce’. The factory therefore explains the courtroom, and ‘the ruling ideas of every age are the ideas of its ruling class’. History advances by contradiction between forces and relations, through slave, feudal, capitalist and communist stages.
, exploitation is given a precise mechanism. By the labour theory of value, labour alone creates value; but the worker sells his
for a subsistence wage while working far longer than needed to reproduce it. Paid for four hours and made to work eight, he yields four hours of unpaid
appropriated as profit. Exploitation is thus not the employer’s cruelty but the structure of wage labour itself.
, which confronts the worker as an alien commodity; from the
, which is monotonous and externally imposed; from his
, the creative social nature that makes him human; and from
, reduced to competitors. The assembly-line worker fitting one bolt all day owns nothing he makes and recognises nothing of himself in it.
4. Class in itself to class for itself.
Classes are defined by relation to the means of production, and ‘the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggle’. But a
— workers who merely share a common position — becomes a

only when it acquires consciousness and organisation: millions of workers are a statistic, an organised proletariat is a force. Only then does revolution follow, the dictatorship of the proletariat intervene and the state ‘wither away’. Yet in the advanced West the revolution never came.
, the ‘theoretician of the superstructure’, answers that the bourgeoisie rules not by force alone but by
— intellectual and moral leadership exercised through
(political society plus civil society, ‘hegemony armoured by coercion’). School, press and church make inequality appear as ‘common sense’. Revolution therefore requires a
— a long counter-hegemonic struggle led by
risen from the class itself — before any ‘war of manoeuvre’.
Gramsci relocates the decisive struggle from economics to
, granting the superstructure relative autonomy and thereby explaining capitalism’s durability without abandoning Marx. He repairs

rather than discarding historical materialism, and in doing so opens the road from classical Marxism to the neo-Marxist analysis of ideology, culture and hegemony pursued by Althusser, the Frankfurt School and subaltern studies.

Q — Critically examine Arendt’s conceptual triad of labour, work and action, her distinction between power and violence, and her conception of ‘the political’ as the antidote to totalitarianism. (UPSC 2019)
Define the three activities, rank them, and show why only the highest one can immunise a society against totalitarian rule.
, endless toil for biological survival, leaving nothing behind.
(Cooking a meal that is eaten and must be cooked again tomorrow.)
, fabricating a durable world of objects.
(The table outlives the dinner — and its maker.)
— the highest: speech and deed among equals, resting on
(A citizens’ assembly arguing in public — beginning something no one could predict.)
— power is ‘acting in concert’ and belongs to a group; violence is instrumental.
(A crowd that refuses to disperse has power; the tank that fires on it has only violence.)
5. Totalitarianism and the banality of evil
— ideology plus terror destroys the plural public realm.
(Eichmann was no monster but a thoughtless clerk who never asked what he was doing.)
— civic republicanism is the antidote, though
and feminists attack her public/private divide.

, which answers the biological necessities of the body — cyclical, repetitive and leaving no trace, like the meal that is cooked, consumed and must be cooked again tomorrow. Because it is compelled by necessity, man is here
; labour sustains life but builds no world.

, who fabricates the durable artifice of things — tables, houses, laws, works of art — that stands between man and nature and gives human life stability and permanence. The table outlives the dinner and its maker. Yet work operates by the means-end logic of the craftsman, treating everything as instrument, and it is carried on in isolation; it therefore cannot supply meaning, only utility.
is the highest activity: speech and deed among equals in a public realm, the only activity that goes on directly between men without the mediation of things. Its conditions are
— ‘men, not Man, live on the earth’ — and its gift is
, the capacity to begin something unpredictable, as in a citizens’ assembly arguing in public. Only through action do we disclose who we are and become
. Modernity inverts this in the ‘victory of the animal laborans’, the ‘rise of the social’ and ‘world alienation’.
, Arendt severs the usual identification of the two. ‘Power corresponds to the human ability not just to act but to act
’; it belongs to a group and ‘exists only so long as the group holds together’, so it is never the property of an individual.

, by contrast, is instrumental and needs implements. ‘Where genuine power is absent, violence may emerge to fill the gap’, and ‘violence can destroy power but is utterly incapable of creating it’ — the crowd that refuses to disperse has power; the tank that fires on it has only violence.
5. Totalitarianism and the banality of evil.
, Arendt shows how ideology plus terror destroys the plural public realm, atomises men into a lonely mass and abolishes the space in which action is possible. The consequence appears in
: the greatest crimes are committed not by monsters but by thoughtless functionaries who never ask what they are doing — evil arising ‘from the absence of sound thinking and judgment’.
Arendt relocates freedom from the private and economic realm to the
of councils and assemblies — the essence of politics and the true antidote to totalitarianism. Critics such as
, feminists and Marxists fault her rigid public/private divide for exiling poverty, labour and gender from politics; yet her warning that thoughtlessness enables evil remains profound.
: justice = functional harmony (myth of metals); philosopher-king; communism of rulers/guardians; ‘state is individual writ large’.
The Open Society and Its Enemies
: ‘Plato was an enemy of the open society’ (totalitarian).
: ‘man is by nature a political animal’; rectified Plato’s idealism; ‘Plato is my friend, but truth a greater friend’.
kingship/tyranny, aristocracy/oligarchy, polity/democracy; polity = golden mean (middle class).
: proportionate equality; ‘inequality real or imagined is the cause of revolution’.
: politics ≠ ethics; lion + fox; virtu vs fortuna (the river in flood); ‘better to be feared than loved’; ‘Galileo of politics’ (Cassirer).
: war of all against all; life ‘nasty, poor, brutish and short’; single contract; absolute sovereign.
: peaceful state of nature; two contracts; natural rights (life, liberty, property); limited ‘trust’ state; labour theory of property.

contentText: Syllabus — Western Political Thought: Plato, Aristotle, Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke, John S. Mill, Marx, Gramsci, Hannah Arendt. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 10) Unit Snapshot What this unit covers:  the canon of Western political thinkers — Plato, Aristotle, Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke, J.S. Mill, Marx, Gramsci and Hannah Arendt — their central ideas, the comparisons the syllabus draws (Plato vs Aristotle, Hobbes vs Locke, Marx vs Gramsci) and their critiques. Must-know anchors:  Plato (justice, philosopher-king, Popper critique), Aristotle (constitutions, revolution), Machiavelli (realism, virtu-fortuna), Hobbes (Leviathan, sovereignty), Locke (natural rights, limited state), Mill (liberty, harm principle), Marx (materialism, alienation, surplus value), Gramsci (hegemony), Arendt (vita activa, banality of evil). PYQ trend:  Plato/Popper (2015), Aristotle (2015/2017/2019/2021), Machiavelli (2014/2018), Hobbes (2017), Mill (2014/2018/2021), Marx (2015/2016/2020), Gramsci (2013/2015/2016/2019), Arendt (2019). Master Questions Q — Examine Plato’s conception of justice, education, communism and the philosopher-king, and evaluate Popper’s charge that ‘Plato was an enemy of the open society’. (UPSC 2015) What it’s asking:  Build Plato’s ideal state — justice, education, philosopher-king, communism — and then judge whether it really amounts to totalitarianism. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Justice  — functional harmony, ‘one man, one job’: each class does its own task and no other.  (The doctor heals, the soldier guards, the farmer farms; injustice is the farmer trying to command the army.) 2. Soul and the myth of metals  — reason/spirit/appetite match rulers/guardians/producers.  (Gold, silver and bronze souls — yet a bronze father may have a gold son, so birth is not destiny.)  ‘The state is the individual writ large’. 3. Education and the philosopher-king  — a lifelong sieve ending at 50 in rule by the wise.  (Allegory of the cave: prisoners mistake shadows on the wall for reality; only he who has left the cave and seen the sun may rule — as one wants the trained navigator at the helm, not the loudest sailor.) 4. Communism of the guardians  — no private property or family for the two ruling classes only.  (A judge who owns no shares in the company before him, and no son to favour, cannot be bought.) 5. Popper’s charge  —  Popper : a closed, unaccountable, change-freezing order.  (Censorship of poets and state-arranged breeding — the closed society in miniature.) 6. Conclusion  — the charge is anachronistic;  Whitehead : all Western philosophy is ‘footnotes to Plato’. Model Answer 1. Justice.  In  The Republic ,  Plato  defines justice as ‘each element in society doing its appropriate task, doing it well and doing it only’ — a  functional harmony  rather than a legal rule. On this ‘one man, one job’ principle the doctor heals, the soldier guards and the farmer produces; injustice is meddling, the farmer presuming to command the army. Justice is thus ‘the architectonic principle’ that holds the whole polis together. 2. Soul and the myth of metals.  The state mirrors the soul: its three parts —  reason, spirit and appetite  — correspond to rulers, guardians and producers, since ‘the state is the individual writ large’. The  myth of the metals  legitimises this order as a ‘noble lie’: men are born with gold, silver or bronze in their souls. Crucially the scheme is not hereditary caste — a bronze artisan’s gifted son may be promoted to gold, so function, not birth, fixes rank. 3. Education and the philosopher-king.  Justice is realised through  state-sponsored education , a lifelong sieve culminating at fifty in the rule of the  philosopher-king  — ‘until philosophers are rulers or rulers learn philosophy, there is no end to the ills of states’. The  allegory of the cave  supplies the justification: chained prisoners take flickering shadows for reality, and only the philosopher who has climbed out and seen the sun knows the Form of the Good. Hence ‘it is foolish to limit an expert physician with the book of medicine’ — the philosopher-king rules by wisdom, not by law. 4. Communism of the guardians.  To free the rulers from private temptation, Plato prescribes  communism of property and of wives  — but only for the two upper classes, the producers keeping both. The logic is the modern conflict-of-interest rule: a judge who owns no shares in the company before him, and has no son to promote, cannot be bought. It is therefore an ‘economic solution to a political ailment’, unlike  Marx’s  economy-wide, economically motivated communism. 5. Popper’s charge.  Karl Popper , in  The Open Society and Its Enemies , holds that ‘Plato was an enemy of the open society’: a rigid class order, censorship of poets and music, state-arranged breeding, and rule by an unaccountable elite add up to  totalitarianism . Above all Plato sought to ‘arrest all political change’ — ‘change is evil, rest divine’ — which is the mark of the closed society.  Bertrand Russell  likewise dubbed Plato a totalitarian. 6. Conclusion.  The charge is powerful but arguably anachronistic, reading twentieth-century fascism back into a fourth-century BC moral treatise;  Levinson  replies that ‘fascism and Platonism are incomparable’, for Plato’s rulers hold no property and seek no glory. Whatever the verdict, his linkage of knowledge, virtue and rule remains the founding statement of political philosophy — all Western philosophy, said  Whitehead , is ‘footnotes to Plato’. Q — Analyse Aristotle’s critique of Plato’s idealism, and contrast their theories of justice and the state. (UPSC 2019) What it’s asking:  Show how the pupil demolished the teacher — on Forms, on ‘one man, one job’ and communism — and then set their justice and state side by side. Gist — the spine to recall 1. The break  — idealism gives way to empirical realism.  (Plato designs the state he wishes existed; Aristotle collects 158 constitutions that actually exist.)  ‘Plato is my friend, but truth is a greater friend’. 2. Against the Forms  — a separate ‘world of ideas’ is unreal; the essence lies inside the thing.  (There is no perfect Chair in heaven — only chairs, studied and classified.) 3. Against ‘one man, one job’ and communism  — both defy human nature.  (‘What is common to the greatest number gets the least care’ — like a shared hostel kitchen nobody cleans.) 4. Justice contrasted  — Plato: inner, moral, duty-based; Aristotle: external, legal,  proportionate .  (Equal pay for equal work, but higher office for higher merit — the seed of reservation debates.) 5. The state contrasted  — both make it the school of the good life, but Plato perfects an ideal, Aristotle improves the actual.  (Philosopher-king vs rule of law and a middle-class polity.) 6. Conclusion  — realism corrects idealism; hence Aristotle, not Plato, is the ‘father of political science’. Model Answer 1. The break.  Aristotle  was Plato’s pupil for twenty years and ‘rectified the limitations of Plato’s ideas’ by replacing idealism with  empirical realism . Where Plato deduces the state he wishes existed from the Form of the Good, Aristotle collects and dissects 158 actual constitutions. The method is captured in ‘Plato is my friend, but truth is a greater friend’ — or, as  Will Durant  puts it, ‘as Brutus loved Rome more, so for Aristotle dear is Plato, but dearer is truth’. 2. Against the Forms.  Aristotle rejects the  theory of Forms  — the claim that a separate, changeless ‘world of ideas’ is more real than the world we inhabit. For him the essence of a thing lies within the thing itself: there is no perfect Chair in heaven, only chairs to be observed, compared and classified. Politics accordingly becomes a practical science of what is attainable for men as they are, not a contemplation of an unrealisable ideal. 3. Against ‘one man, one job’ and communism.  Plato’s functional justice is faulted as  monotonous , too subjective and moral rather than legal, and as stressing duties while ignoring rights. His  communism of wives and property  fares worse: ‘what is common to the greatest number gets the least care’ — everyone’s property is no one’s responsibility, as in a shared hostel kitchen nobody cleans. Aristotle defends private property as the spur to effort and the family as a ‘time-tested institution’ of emotional stability. 4. Justice contrasted.  For Plato justice is  inner, moral and spiritual  — the harmony of the soul, a matter of performing duties. For Aristotle it is  external, legal and practical , resting on  proportionate equality : ‘it is unjust to treat equals unequally and unequals equally’. Equal work earns equal pay, but greater merit earns greater office — the ancestor of every modern argument over merit and compensatory discrimination. He splits it into  distributive  and  corrective  justice. 5. The state contrasted.  Both hold the state essential to the good life — Plato aims at ‘the greatest happiness of the whole’, Aristotle declares ‘man is by nature a political animal’ and the state exists ‘for the sake of the good life’. But Plato is the  idealist  who designs an ideal polis ruled by philosopher-kings above the law, while Aristotle is the  pragmatic realist  who prefers the rule of law and a middle-class ‘polity’ as the most stable attainable form. 6. Conclusion.  Aristotle’s realism corrects Plato’s idealism — the shift is from an ideal to be constructed to institutions to be observed, compared and improved — which is why he, and not Plato, is called the ‘father of political science’. Yet the correction is internal to a shared Socratic conviction: the state exists not for mere life but for human excellence. Q — Explain Aristotle’s classification of constitutions, his theory of proportionate equality and revolution, and assess his contribution to modern constitutional democracy. (UPSC 2021/2017) What it’s asking:  Give the two criteria and the six forms, defend polity, then link proportionate equality and the causes of revolution to modern constitutionalism. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Two criteria  — how many rule, and for whose benefit.  (A single ruler serving the people is a king; the same man serving himself is a tyrant.) 2. Six constitutions  — one:  kingship/tyranny ; few:  aristocracy/oligarchy ; many:  polity/democracy .  (For Aristotle ‘democracy’ is the perverted form — rule by the poor in their own interest.) 3. Polity, the golden mean  — the middle class buffers rich and poor.  (A society of billionaires and beggars flips between oligarchy and mob rule; a large middle class steadies it.) 4. Proportionate equality  — equals equally, unequals unequally in proportion.  (Distributive: offices by merit; corrective: the court restores what was taken, whoever the parties are.) 5. Revolution  — ‘the feeling of inequality, real or imagined, is the cause of revolution’.  (Perception is enough: a group that merely believes it is being denied its due will rebel.) 6. Contribution and conclusion  — rule of law, mixed government and stability seed modern constitutionalism, though his exclusions must go. Model Answer 1. Two criteria.  Aristotle , the ‘father of comparative politics’, who with his students examined 158 constitutions, classifies governments on two axes: the  number of rulers  — one, few or many — and the  end served , whether the common good or the rulers’ own interest. The second is decisive: one man ruling for his people is a king, the same man ruling for himself is a tyrant. Form alone never settles legitimacy. 2. Six constitutions.  The cross-classification yields three correct forms and their perversions: rule by one —  Kingship  against  Tyranny ; by few —  Aristocracy  against  Oligarchy ; by many —  Polity  against  Democracy . The last pair surprises modern readers: for Aristotle ‘democracy’ is the debased form, rule by the poor majority in their own class interest, whereas polity is the many ruling for the common good. 3. Polity, the golden mean.  Polity is the ‘golden mean’ between oligarchy and democracy, and Aristotle identifies it with the  middle class . Neither so rich as to be arrogant nor so poor as to be servile, it is the class most amenable to reason and to law. A society polarised between billionaires and beggars oscillates between oligarchy and mob rule; a broad middle stratum moderates the conflict and makes the constitution both stable and practicable — the best form for most states most of the time. 4. Proportionate equality.  Justice requires ‘treating equals equally and unequals unequally in proportion to their inequalities’ —  proportionate, not absolute, equality . It works through  distributive justice , which allots honours and offices according to merit and contribution to the polis, and  corrective justice , which simply restores what has been wrongly taken, treating the parties as arithmetically equal. The distinction remains the backbone of every argument about equity versus formal equality. 5. Revolution.  ‘The feeling of inequality, real or imagined, is the cause of revolution’, and ‘poverty is the parent of revolution and crime’. The insight is psychological rather than economic: perception suffices, so a group that merely believes it is denied its due will revolt. Aristotle catalogues general and regime-specific causes and cures, counselling moderation, obedience to law, and enlargement of the middle class — a conservative concern for  stability . 6. Contribution and conclusion.  His insistence on the  rule of law  over the rule of persons — ‘law is reason without passion’ — his mixed, middle-class polity and his focus on constitutional stability directly anticipate modern constitutional democracy, and reach India through the basic-structure idea of a government limited by law. His exclusion of women, workers and slaves from citizenship is ‘unacceptable in modern times’; democratise the citizen body and the framework survives intact. Q — Critically examine Machiavelli’s separation of politics from ethics and religion, and his place in the evolution of political science. (UPSC 2018/2014) What it’s asking:  Explain why he cuts politics loose from morality and the Church, then judge what that did for the discipline. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Realist premise  — men are selfish and fickle, so theorise them as they are.  (‘Men sooner forget the death of their father than the loss of their patrimony’.) 2. Politics vs ethics — the lion and the fox  — the prince ‘needs to know how to be bad’.  (The lion frightens off wolves but walks into traps; the fox sees the trap but cannot fight wolves — a ruler needs force and cunning together.) 3. Virtu and fortuna  — skill mastering chance.  (Fortuna is a river in flood: dykes built in calm weather — virtu — decide whether it drowns you.) 4. Politics vs religion  — religion is a tool of civic discipline: ‘use religion, don’t get used by it’.  (An oath binds a soldier where a wage will not.) 5. Place in political science  — the empirical method applied to states ‘as they are, not as they ought to be’;  Cassirer : the ‘Galileo of politics’. 6. Critique and conclusion  — amoral cynic ( Maxey ), dated to Renaissance Italy ( Sabine ), a ‘death trap’ ( Gandhi ) — yet all practise him. Model Answer 1. Realist premise.  Writing in  The Prince  amid the chaos of Renaissance Italy,  Machiavelli  founds  political realism  on a bleak reading of human nature: men are ungrateful, fickle and acquisitive, and ‘sooner forget the death of their father than the loss of their patrimony’. Political theory must therefore be built on men as they are, not as scripture wishes them to be — the first premise of every subsequent realist, from Hobbes to Morgenthau. 2. Politics vs ethics — the lion and the fox.  Judging action by  results  rather than morality, he holds that the prince ‘needs to know how to be bad rather than good’ and must combine ‘the courage of the  lion  with the cunning of the  fox ’, changing colours ‘like a chameleon’. The image is exact: the lion frightens off wolves but blunders into traps, the fox spots the trap but cannot fight wolves — force without guile, or guile without force, both fail. Hence, on the safer bet, ‘it is better for a prince to be  feared than loved ’. 3. Virtu and fortuna.  Success is the product of  virtu  — not Christian virtue but energy, foresight and manly skill — contending with  fortuna , the element of chance in politics. Machiavelli likens fortuna to a river in flood: it cannot be abolished, but embankments raised in calm weather decide whether it drowns you. Roughly half of human affairs is thus governed by fortune and half left to our own control — a rejection of both divine providence and fatalism. 4. Politics vs religion.  Machiavelli treats religion  instrumentally : not as truth to be obeyed but as a unifying, disciplining force to be managed, so that the ruler should ‘use religion rather than get used by it’. An oath binds a soldier where a wage will not, and Roman civic religion made citizens brave, whereas Christian otherworldliness had, he thought, made Italians weak. This subordination of Church to state makes him the ‘father of European secularism’. 5. Place in political science.  By applying the  empirical, historical method  to human affairs — studying states ‘as they are, not as they ought to be’ and reasoning from Roman and Italian example — Machiavelli breaks decisively with medieval theology and makes politics an autonomous, observable domain.  Ernst Cassirer  therefore called him ‘the Galileo of politics’; if Machiavelli was Copernicus,  Hobbes  was the Galileo of political theory. 6. Critique and conclusion.  He is condemned as ‘the most universally reprobated figure’ ( Maxey ), an amoral cynic who licenses cruelty;  Sabine  finds him ‘narrowly dated and narrowly located’ in the Italy of city-state warfare; and  Gandhi  saw the divorce of ethics from politics as a ‘death trap’. Yet the realism endures because it describes practice: as  Dunning  observed, ‘everyone practises Machiavellism without confessing it’. Q — Discuss Hobbes’ derivation of the state from human nature and the state of nature, his theory of absolute sovereignty and political obligation, and compare him with Machiavelli. (UPSC 2017) What it’s asking:  Trace the chain — human nature to state of nature to contract to absolute sovereign — then say how this differs from Machiavelli’s realism. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Human nature  — ‘an endless desire for power after power that ceases only in death’, driven by fear.  (‘Fear and I were born twins’ — Hobbes was born as the Armada approached.) 2. State of nature  — a ‘war of every man against every man’; life ‘solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short’.  (Not a jungle but a blackout riot: no police, so even the peaceable arm themselves first.) 3. The single contract  — all with all, surrendering every right at once; society and state are born together.  (The sovereign is not a party, so he can breach nothing.) 4. Absolute sovereignty  — ‘absolute, indivisible, inalienable, perpetual’; ‘covenants without the sword are but words’.  (No division of powers: a Leviathan cut in two is two civil wars.) 5. Political obligation  — total and irrevocable, yet resting on  self-preservation .  (A conscript may flee the battlefield; if the state cannot protect you, it cannot command you.) 6. Hobbes vs Machiavelli and conclusion  — advice to a prince versus a deductive science of the state;  Macpherson : ‘possessive individualism’. Model Answer 1. Human nature.  Using the ‘resolutive-compositive’ method borrowed from Galileo — break society into its parts, then rebuild it —  Hobbes  derives the state logically from  human nature . Man is matter in motion, selfish and materialistic, marked by ‘an endless desire for power after power that ceases only in death’, and above all governed by  fear . Born as the Spanish Armada approached, he wrote that ‘fear and I were born twins’ — fear is the engine of the whole system. 2. State of nature.  Absent a common power to keep men in awe, natural equality of ability breeds equality of hope, and hope breeds conflict: the result is a  ‘war of every man against every man’  fuelled by competition, diffidence and glory, in which life is ‘solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short’. It is less a jungle than a city blackout: with no police, even the peaceable must strike first to be safe. Right and wrong have no place; there is only right of nature to everything. 3. The single contract.  Escape comes through reason — the laws of nature counselling peace — executed by a  single contract  in which each man covenants with every other, not with the ruler, to surrender  all  his natural rights to a common power. Society and state are thus created in one stroke, with no pre-political community as in Locke. Because the sovereign is not a party to the covenant, he can never be accused of breaching it — the device that makes his power unchallengeable. 4. Absolute sovereignty.  The  sovereign, the Leviathan  — ‘that mortal god’ — is ‘absolute, indivisible, inalienable and perpetual’, at once legislator, judge and head of the church. ‘Law is the command of the sovereign’, anticipating  Austin ’s legal positivism, and ‘covenants without the sword are but words and of no strength to secure a man at all’. Division of powers is fatal: a Leviathan cut in two is simply two civil wars. 5. Political obligation.  Since the covenant binds subjects to one another, obligation to obey is  total and irrevocable ; there is no right of revolt and ‘liberty exists where the law is silent’. Yet the whole edifice rests on consent given for  self-preservation , so the one right that cannot be alienated is the right to life: a condemned man may resist and a conscript may flee the battlefield. If the sovereign cannot protect, he cannot command — protection and obedience are reciprocal. 6. Hobbes vs Machiavelli and conclusion.  Both are  realists  who reject natural sociability and moralised politics, but  Machiavelli  offers  prudential advice to a prince  whose end is glory and survival, while  Hobbes  builds a  systematic, deductive science  of the state whose end is escape from the state of nature.  Macpherson  reads him as the theorist of ‘possessive individualism’ fitting a market society — yet by grounding authority in consent, Hobbes is paradoxically a father of modern individualism. Q — Evaluate Locke as the father of liberalism through his two contracts, natural rights, labour theory of property and toleration; and contrast with Hobbes on how each legitimizes state authority. What it’s asking:  Show how Locke’s milder premises produce a limited state, then set his justification of authority against Hobbes’s point by point. Gist — the spine to recall 1. State of nature  — peaceful and social, spoilt only by two ‘inconveniences’.  (No impartial judge: even an honest man judging his own boundary dispute will overvalue his claim.) 2. Two contracts  — one creates society, a second creates government by consent.  (Society survives the fall of a government, as a nation outlives a dissolved Parliament.) 3. Natural rights and the trust state  — life, liberty and property are retained, not surrendered; power is a  trust .  (A trustee who loots the estate is dismissed — hence the right of revolution.) 4. Labour theory of property  — ‘property is the product of one’s labour’, limited by spoilage and ‘enough and as good’ left for others.  (The apple is mine because I picked it, not because the king granted it.) 5. Toleration  — the magistrate has no jurisdiction over the soul.  (But not for atheists, whose oaths he thought worthless.) 6. Hobbes vs Locke and conclusion  — absolute versus limited: ‘liberty where the law is silent’ against ‘no law, no liberty’. Model Answer 1. State of nature.  Locke , the ‘father of liberalism’, begins from a  balanced human nature  in which reason — the law of nature — teaches men ‘not to harm others in their life, liberty and property’. His  state of nature  is therefore ‘a state of peace and mutual assistance’, pre-political but not pre-social, flawed only by two  inconveniences : each man judges his own cause, and passion distorts punishment. Even an honest man judging his own boundary dispute overvalues his claim — so an impartial judge, not a Leviathan, is what is wanted. 2. Two contracts.  Men accordingly make  two contracts : the first constitutes civil society, the second institutes a government by  consent , to which they transfer only the powers to make, execute and adjudicate law. The separation matters constitutionally: because society precedes government, the fall of a government does not dissolve the community — a nation outlives a dissolved Parliament — and a people may replace its rulers without returning to anarchy. 3. Natural rights and the trust state.  Rights to  life, liberty and property  are inalienable and are carried into civil society, not surrendered to it. The state therefore holds  delegated, fiduciary (trust) power , never original power: a ‘night-watchman’ state whose ‘sole purpose is the protection of property’, organised through separated legislative, executive and federative powers with the legislature supreme. A trustee who loots the estate is dismissed — which is precisely Locke’s  right of revolution . 4. Labour theory of property.  Property is pre-political and moral: ‘every man has a property in his own person’, so by mixing his labour with nature he makes a thing his own. The apple is mine because I picked it, not because the sovereign granted it. Two limits apply — no accumulation beyond what one can use without  spoilage , and ‘enough and as good’ must be left for others — though the invention of money quietly relaxes both, which is why  Macpherson  reads him as legitimising unlimited accumulation. 5. Toleration.  In the  Letter Concerning Toleration , Locke separates the ends of the state from those of the church: the magistrate governs ‘civil interests’ alone and has no jurisdiction over the soul, since belief cannot be coerced into existence by force. The principle is the seed of the modern secular state and of freedom of conscience — though he notoriously excludes atheists, whose oaths he thought worthless, and Catholics, as owing allegiance abroad. 6. Hobbes vs Locke and conclusion.  Both argue from contract, but from opposite premises:  Hobbes  — a war-like state of nature, a  single contract , no rights retained, an  absolute  sovereign, ‘liberty where the law is silent’;  Locke  — a peaceful state of nature,  two contracts , inalienable rights, a  limited  state, ‘where there is no law there is no liberty’. Hobbes legitimises authority as absolute to escape chaos; Locke legitimises it as limited and accountable to secure pre-existing rights — founding the liberal-constitutional tradition that runs to Rawls. Q — Assess Mill’s harm principle and defence of free expression, his status as a ‘reluctant democrat’, and his case for the equality of women, within his revision of utilitarianism. (UPSC 2014/2018/2021) What it’s asking:  Four demands in one: how he rewrote utilitarianism, and how liberty, democracy and women’s equality follow from it. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Qualitative utilitarianism  — pleasures differ in kind, not only in quantity.  (‘Better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied’ — poetry outranks pushpin, rescuing Bentham from the ‘pig’s philosophy’.) 2. Harm principle  — your liberty ends only where it harms another.  (Drinking alone is self-regarding and free; drunk driving harms others and may be punished.) 3. Free expression  — ‘all silencing of discussion is an assumption of infallibility’.  (Even one dissenter must be heard: the silenced opinion may be true, or hold part of the truth.) 4. Reluctant democrat  — he fears the  tyranny of the majority  and prescribes plural voting and PR.  (A graduate’s extra vote — quality checking mere numbers.) 5. Subjection of women  — legal subordination is ‘one of the chief hindrances to human improvement’.  (‘There remains no legal slave save the mistress of every house’.) 6. Conclusion  — the ‘first serious liberal democrat’ ( Macpherson ), though  Barker  calls his liberty empty. Model Answer 1. Qualitative utilitarianism.  Mill  rescues utilitarianism by adding a  qualitative  dimension: pleasures differ in kind, and those who have known both prefer the higher — ‘it is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied’. Against  Bentham’s  claim that pushpin equals poetry if the quantity of pleasure is equal, this restores a standard of human excellence and disarms the charge of a ‘pig’s philosophy’. 2. Harm principle.  In  On Liberty  Mill gives liberty priority: ‘over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign’. The  harm principle  holds that ‘the sole end for which mankind is warranted in interfering with the liberty of a person is to prevent harm to others’ — a man’s own good is never sufficient warrant. Drinking alone is self-regarding and free; drunk driving is other-regarding and punishable. Liberty ends exactly where it harms another. 3. Free expression.  Mill’s defence of discussion is absolute: ‘all silencing of discussion is an assumption of infallibility’, and if all mankind minus one held an opinion, mankind would be no more justified in silencing that one than he in silencing mankind. The silenced view may be true; if false, truth held unchallenged decays into ‘dead dogma’; usually each side holds part of the truth. Hence his defence of the eccentric ‘crank’, whose rare genius benefits mankind. 4. Reluctant democrat.  C.L. Wayper  calls Mill a  ‘reluctant democrat’ : he accepts representative government as the ideal form yet fears the  tyranny of the majority  — the social coercion of opinion that  Tocqueville  had diagnosed in  Democracy in America . His safeguards favour quality over mere numbers: plural or weighted voting for the educated, proportional representation to protect minorities, open ballot, and a strong second chamber. 5. Subjection of women.  In  The Subjection of Women , written with  Harriet Taylor’s  influence, Mill attacks the legal subordination of women as ‘one of the chief hindrances to human improvement’ and observes that ‘there remains no legal slave save the mistress of every house’. Equality would end the family as ‘a school of despotism’, make it instead a school of sympathy, and ‘double the mass of mental faculties available for the higher service of humanity’. He moved the first parliamentary amendment for women’s suffrage. 6. Conclusion.  Mill is the ‘first serious liberal democrat’ ( Macpherson ), balancing utility with liberty, majority rule with minority rights, and individuality with social progress.  Barker  faults the self- and other-regarding distinction as untenable — no act is purely private — making him a ‘prophet of an empty liberty’; yet the harm principle remains the working test of state interference in every modern debate on censorship, privacy and personal choice. Q — Discuss Marx’s base-superstructure model, class and class struggle, and alienation; and how Gramsci’s concepts of hegemony, the integral state and organic intellectuals rescued Marxism from economic determinism. (UPSC 2015/2016/2020 + Gramsci 2013/2016/2019) What it’s asking:  First lay out classical Marxism, then show precisely which of its defects Gramsci repairs and how. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Base and superstructure  — who owns production shapes law, politics and ideas.  (‘To think we must live, to live we must eat, and to eat we must produce’ — the factory explains the courtroom.) 2. Surplus value  — labour alone creates value; the capitalist pockets the unpaid remainder.  (Paid for four hours, worked for eight — the other four are profit.) 3. Alienation  — estrangement from the product, the process, others and oneself.  (The assembly-line worker who fits one bolt all day owns nothing he makes and recognises nothing of himself in it.) 4. Class in itself to class for itself  — revolution needs consciousness, not just misery.  (Millions of workers are a statistic; an organised, self-aware proletariat is a force.)  But the predicted revolution never came. 5. Gramsci’s hegemony  — rule by consent through civil society, the ‘integral state’.  (School, press and church make inequality look like common sense — so fight a  war of position  led by organic intellectuals before the war of manoeuvre.) 6. Conclusion  — the decisive battlefield shifts from economics to culture; determinism is repaired, not abandoned. Model Answer 1. Base and superstructure.  Marx’s   historical materialism  holds that the economic  base  — the forces and relations of production — conditions the  superstructure  of law, state, religion and ideas: ‘in order to think we must live, to live we must eat, and to eat we must produce’. The factory therefore explains the courtroom, and ‘the ruling ideas of every age are the ideas of its ruling class’. History advances by contradiction between forces and relations, through slave, feudal, capitalist and communist stages. 2. Surplus value.  In  Das Kapital , exploitation is given a precise mechanism. By the labour theory of value, labour alone creates value; but the worker sells his  labour power  for a subsistence wage while working far longer than needed to reproduce it. Paid for four hours and made to work eight, he yields four hours of unpaid  surplus value  appropriated as profit. Exploitation is thus not the employer’s cruelty but the structure of wage labour itself. 3. Alienation.  In the  Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts , Marx describes capitalist labour as  alienating  at four levels: from the  product , which confronts the worker as an alien commodity; from the  process , which is monotonous and externally imposed; from his  species-being , the creative social nature that makes him human; and from  other men , reduced to competitors. The assembly-line worker fitting one bolt all day owns nothing he makes and recognises nothing of himself in it. 4. Class in itself to class for itself.  Classes are defined by relation to the means of production, and ‘the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggle’. But a  class in itself  — workers who merely share a common position — becomes a  class for itself  only when it acquires consciousness and organisation: millions of workers are a statistic, an organised proletariat is a force. Only then does revolution follow, the dictatorship of the proletariat intervene and the state ‘wither away’. Yet in the advanced West the revolution never came. 5. Gramsci’s hegemony.  Gramsci , the ‘theoretician of the superstructure’, answers that the bourgeoisie rules not by force alone but by  hegemony  — intellectual and moral leadership exercised through  civil society , the consent-wing of the  integral state  (political society plus civil society, ‘hegemony armoured by coercion’). School, press and church make inequality appear as ‘common sense’. Revolution therefore requires a  war of position  — a long counter-hegemonic struggle led by  organic intellectuals  risen from the class itself — before any ‘war of manoeuvre’. 6. Conclusion.  Gramsci relocates the decisive struggle from economics to  culture and consciousness , granting the superstructure relative autonomy and thereby explaining capitalism’s durability without abandoning Marx. He repairs  economic determinism  rather than discarding historical materialism, and in doing so opens the road from classical Marxism to the neo-Marxist analysis of ideology, culture and hegemony pursued by Althusser, the Frankfurt School and subaltern studies. Q — Critically examine Arendt’s conceptual triad of labour, work and action, her distinction between power and violence, and her conception of ‘the political’ as the antidote to totalitarianism. (UPSC 2019) What it’s asking:  Define the three activities, rank them, and show why only the highest one can immunise a society against totalitarian rule. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Labour  — the  animal laborans , endless toil for biological survival, leaving nothing behind.  (Cooking a meal that is eaten and must be cooked again tomorrow.) 2. Work  — the  homo faber , fabricating a durable world of objects.  (The table outlives the dinner — and its maker.) 3. Action  — the highest: speech and deed among equals, resting on  freedom, plurality and natality .  (A citizens’ assembly arguing in public — beginning something no one could predict.) 4. Power vs violence  — power is ‘acting in concert’ and belongs to a group; violence is instrumental.  (A crowd that refuses to disperse has power; the tank that fires on it has only violence.) 5. Totalitarianism and the banality of evil  — ideology plus terror destroys the plural public realm.  (Eichmann was no monster but a thoughtless clerk who never asked what he was doing.) 6. Conclusion  — civic republicanism is the antidote, though  Benhabib  and feminists attack her public/private divide. Model Answer 1. Labour.  In  The Human Condition ,  Arendt  divides the  vita activa  into three. The lowest is  labour , the activity of the  animal laborans , which answers the biological necessities of the body — cyclical, repetitive and leaving no trace, like the meal that is cooked, consumed and must be cooked again tomorrow. Because it is compelled by necessity, man is here  unfree ; labour sustains life but builds no world. 2. Work.  Work  is the activity of  homo faber , who fabricates the durable artifice of things — tables, houses, laws, works of art — that stands between man and nature and gives human life stability and permanence. The table outlives the dinner and its maker. Yet work operates by the means-end logic of the craftsman, treating everything as instrument, and it is carried on in isolation; it therefore cannot supply meaning, only utility. 3. Action.  Action  is the highest activity: speech and deed among equals in a public realm, the only activity that goes on directly between men without the mediation of things. Its conditions are  freedom  and  plurality  — ‘men, not Man, live on the earth’ — and its gift is  natality , the capacity to begin something unpredictable, as in a citizens’ assembly arguing in public. Only through action do we disclose who we are and become  zoon politikon . Modernity inverts this in the ‘victory of the animal laborans’, the ‘rise of the social’ and ‘world alienation’. 4. Power vs violence.  In  On Violence , Arendt severs the usual identification of the two. ‘Power corresponds to the human ability not just to act but to act  in concert ’; it belongs to a group and ‘exists only so long as the group holds together’, so it is never the property of an individual.  Violence , by contrast, is instrumental and needs implements. ‘Where genuine power is absent, violence may emerge to fill the gap’, and ‘violence can destroy power but is utterly incapable of creating it’ — the crowd that refuses to disperse has power; the tank that fires on it has only violence. 5. Totalitarianism and the banality of evil.  In  The Origins of Totalitarianism , Arendt shows how ideology plus terror destroys the plural public realm, atomises men into a lonely mass and abolishes the space in which action is possible. The consequence appears in  Eichmann in Jerusalem  as the  banality of evil : the greatest crimes are committed not by monsters but by thoughtless functionaries who never ask what they are doing — evil arising ‘from the absence of sound thinking and judgment’. 6. Conclusion.  Arendt relocates freedom from the private and economic realm to the  public realm of action , making active participation — a revived  civic republicanism  of councils and assemblies — the essence of politics and the true antidote to totalitarianism. Critics such as  Benhabib , feminists and Marxists fault her rigid public/private divide for exiling poverty, labour and gender from politics; yet her warning that thoughtlessness enables evil remains profound.
